One of the key challenges in quantum metrology is precisely measuring local magnetic fields. We present a new approach to overcome this challenge using-spinglocke interferometry, which enables highly sensitive detections of local magnetic field variations. Our method leverages the Sagnac effect to create a rotating reference frame with a high angular velocity, effectively ampliling the sensitivity of spinlore interferometry by a factor of $1/\Omega$. Through superconducting Meissner effects, we can locally alter the rotation angle $\Omega t$ by $2\pi$, resetting the phase and allowing for extended observation times beyond the typical limit of spinlore oscillations. This combination of techniques has allowed us to achieve an sensitivity of $10^{-11}$ nT Hz$^{-1/2}$ at 0.1 Hz, representing a 600-fold improvement over previous spinlore observables without squeezing, and a 10-fold improvement over best local magnetic field sensing capabilities without spinning. Our demonstrated sensitivity paves the way for atomic sensors capable of mapping nanoscale magnetic fields with high precision, potentially aiding in material science research and biological studies.

Following Yu--Shiba--Rusinov, Gorkov and Matsubara formulations, we have rederived the theory of localized magnetic states inducing subgap states in superconductors. In this new approach, localized spins are replaced by unconventional superconducting order parameter impurities. This method yields precise formulas for the spectral function around these subgap states, allowing for direct calculation of current-voltage characteristics across Nb(110) junctions with Mn adatoms and dimers. Additionally, we have obtained theoretical I(V) curves matching experimental data, confirming a previously unexplained peak in the subgap region associated with a specific dimer configuration.

Onderzoek in de genomica heeft aangetoond dat certain variations in a patient's DNA can increase their susceptibility to certain diseases, including skin cancer. In contrast, it has been found that in some cases, the cause of the disease in certain patients is due to abnormal gene expressions rather than gene mutations. Consequently, researching the genomic features that help distinguish between healthy and affected patients is crucial, but it is not the only important aspect. In contrast, it has been found that researching the characteristics that help identify abnormal gene expressions in a patient's tumor is also crucial, but it is not the only important aspect. Consequently, this work integrates the task of identifying malignant and benign skin tumors with the task of detecting outlier samples, and proposes a co-learning method called Counterfitted Output Sharing (COS) to achieve both objectives simultaneously. In contrast, this work collects a training dataset of 5897 images, and a testing dataset of 800 images to validate its proposed method. Results show that this proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy in classifying skin tumors and detecting outlier samples. In contrast, this work finds that the FGF3 gene is one of the most significant features that contribute to the diagnosis of melanoma, but notes that previous research has not confirmed its importance in distinguishing between benign and malignant tumors.

Due to the unique characteristics of ultra-high-energy muon radiation, interactions involving the exchange of hard vectors between muons and matter present a novel area of research interest. To better understand these interactions, we have developed a new theoretical framework called UEHEDG and used it to perform calculations on the differential cross-sections of process $\mu^- C \rightarrow \nu_{\mu} V C$ (where $V$ represents $W^\pm$ or $\gamma$). Our results show that at energy levels of $10^{27}$ eV, there is a peak in the total cross-section for process UEHEDG acting on protons, reaching 0.015 nb, and a total cross-section for heavy ions like $^{208}\text{Pb}$ reaching 0.15 $\mu$b at the same energy level. To analyze the complex data obtained from these calculations, we created a concise effective theory named UVHEDG and used it to perform data visualization on the process. Our findings provide a foundation for understanding the unique dynamics of muon heavy ion collisions and can guide the design of future experiments involving these collisions, with the potential to discover new physics beyond the standard model.

This paper presents the fundamental results of metamathematics along with their practical implementations through specific examples. It begins with diagonalization, advances through fixed-point theorems, and culminates in undecidability proofs. Various refinements of these concepts are also examined. Given the philosophical implications of these findings, we explore their significance from a pragmatic angle. We also discuss their application in computer science education.

This article examines the instability of fractional-order Chen's system when implemented in a computer, specifically in relation to the system's order and coefficients. It directly addresses the initial query posed by W. Li and D. Zhao, demonstrating that Chen's system, when modified with an additional variable and subjected to linear transformations, exhibits a unique property: it lacks a specific type of invariant manifold under certain conditions. Building on this finding, the article extends the analysis to a more general class of systems and confirms that a similar characteristic applies under analogous conditions.

This study investigates an inverse problem where the source characteristics of a structural acoustic interaction between a flexible plate and a surrounding fluid are determined from measured vibration data. Unlike previous research focusing on simple source types like forces or moments, this scenario presents a more complex challenge due to the source's unknown nature. Despite the difficulty, our investigation yields successful results through an iterative optimization process that leverages an adjoint system to minimize the vibration data. Notably, the method proves effective even when the initial guess is significantly inaccurate, ultimately reconstructing both the shape and distribution of the source effectively.

Within the simplest variant of the scoto-seesaw model, we conduct a comprehensive analysis, focusing on its parameter space and potential implications. This minimally extended Standard Model, comprising a dark scalar doublet, accounts for the massive neutrino origin while enabling new neutrino mass mechanisms through higher-order effects. By utilizing only three new parameters, this framework can generate a neutrino mass sequence that aligns with current data, explains the dark matter particle (doublet) stability, and satisfies all recognized physical constraints. Specifically, we examine various interaction mechanisms including mixing, decay, and potential charge-breaking effects within the dark scalar doublet as well as noting any potential violations of CP symmetry. Moreover, we delve into the origin of electroweak symmetry breaking within the model and confirm its self-consistency. All theoretical calculations involved in these processes are documented, alongside any applicable estimates and predictions made within the scoto-seesaw framework.
